notes: Replog program library — full merged set (batches 1-5). Original structured syntheses of established, freely-documented training methodologies; principles stated in plain language. Not medical advice.

programs.name: Foundation: Full-Body Linear Progression
programs.whoIsItFor: Complete beginners or returners after a long layoff who want the fastest strength gains with minimal time commitment.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with untreated back, knee, or shoulder injuries; post-surgical trainees without clearance.

slots.intensity: add 5kg per session, single top set

programs.schedule: Alternate A/B/A, B/A/B on non-consecutive days (e.g. Mon/Wed/Fri).

progression.rule: Add load every session while all reps complete. On 3 consecutive failures at a weight, deload that lift 10% and rebuild.
progression.deload: Automatic per-lift 10% on stall.

programs.scienceRationale: Novices adapt session-to-session, so per-session load increments capture the fastest possible strength curve. Full-body 3x/week gives each muscle ~9 hard sets and 3 weekly exposures, above the minimum-effective volume threshold and at a frequency shown to benefit strength. Compound-first ordering maximizes skill practice on the highest-value lifts.
evidence: Weekly hard sets and muscle growth rise together
Multi-joint strength takes off once a muscle gets at least six hard sets a week
Strength improves when the same volume is spread over more sessions
programs.expectedResults: Most beginners add 40-80% to squat/deadlift working weights in 12 weeks alongside visible muscle gain.
programs.cautions: Form before load: film sets or get a coach check in weeks 1-2.

programs.name: Upper/Lower Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters past the beginner stage who can train 4 days and want balanced size and strength.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: True beginners (full-body progresses faster); those who can only train 2-3 days.
programs.schedule: Upper/Lower/rest/Upper/Lower/rest/rest.

progression.rule: Work up within the rep range; when the top of the range is hit on all sets, add load next session.
progression.deload: Every 6th week halve set count at same loads.

programs.scienceRationale: Twice-weekly frequency per muscle with 10-16 weekly hard sets sits in the volume band associated with superior hypertrophy while keeping per-session volume recoverable. Mixed rep bands cover both mechanical-tension-dominant and metabolite-dominant stimulus ranges.
evidence: Training a muscle twice a week beats once for the same weekly volume
12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band for growth
Growth rises with weekly sets, but each added set returns a little less
programs.expectedResults: Steady measurable size gains and continued strength PRs over the 10 weeks.
programs.cautions: Volume-bias days should never be to failure on compounds.

programs.name: Push / Pull / Legs (6-Day)
programs.whoIsItFor: Committed lifters with 6 available days chasing maximum muscle.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with under 5 training days, poor sleep, or high life stress — recovery is the limiter.
programs.schedule: Push/Pull/Legs repeated twice, one rest day (e.g. Sun). Second rotation uses different exercise choices per slot.

progression.rule: Top of rep range on all sets -> add load. Rotate exercise variants between rotations to spread joint stress.
progression.deload: Week 8 is a deload: 50% of sets at same loads, then repeat or switch programs.

programs.scienceRationale: Splitting by movement function lets each muscle be trained hard twice weekly with 15-20+ weekly sets — the upper end of the productive volume range — while distributing systemic fatigue across six shorter sessions. High-set approaches show the strongest hypertrophy returns in trained lifters, with diminishing returns managed by the built-in deload.
evidence: 12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band, with smaller muscles favouring its top end
Trained lifters need higher weekly volume to keep growing
Growth rises with weekly sets, but each added set returns a little less
programs.expectedResults: Peak-rate muscle gain for recovered intermediates; strength maintained or slowly built.
programs.cautions: The first sign of accumulating fatigue (sleep, joints, motivation) means pull volume back ~20%.

programs.name: Wave Strength 4-Day (5/3/1-style)
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters whose linear progression has stalled and who want slow, sustainable strength on the big four lifts.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Beginners (leaves gains on the table); pure physique-focused trainees.

monthlyWave.week1: 3x5 @ 65/75/85% of training max, last set AMRAP
monthlyWave.week2: 3x3 @ 70/80/90% of training max, last set AMRAP
monthlyWave.week3: 5/3/1 @ 75/85/95% of training max, last set AMRAP

programs.schedule: 4 lifting days spread across the week; wave advances weekly.

progression.rule: Training max = 90% of true 1RM. After each 4-week wave add 2.5kg to upper-body TMs, 5kg to lower-body TMs. AMRAP sets gauge readiness.
progression.deload: Built into week 4 of every wave.

programs.scienceRationale: Submaximal percentage waves with a monthly progression cadence match the slower adaptation rate of intermediates; planned deloads manage accumulated fatigue, and AMRAP sets autoregulate load prescription against daily readiness. Strength responds strongly to frequency and specificity of heavy practice on the target lifts.
evidence: Strength improves when the same volume is spread over more sessions
Moderate-to-high weekly set counts build multi-joint strength best
Waves of rising load followed by a lighter week outperform a flat grind
programs.expectedResults: 5-15kg added to each big-lift 1RM over 12 weeks for a typical intermediate.
programs.cautions: Never max out during the program; the AMRAP is the test.

programs.name: Lean Engine: Full-Body Fat Loss
programs.whoIsItFor: People in a calorie deficit who want to keep muscle while maximizing energy expenditure in 3 sessions.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone chasing maximal strength PRs mid-deficit; uncontrolled hypertension (circuit format spikes heart rate).

days.name: Circuit A (3 rounds, 60s rest between rounds)

programs.schedule: A/B/A one week, B/A/B the next, non-consecutive days; 8-10k daily steps strongly encouraged.

progression.rule: First shorten round rest 60s -> 45s -> 30s across weeks, then add load and reset rest.
progression.deload: Week 5: two rounds only.

programs.scienceRationale: In a deficit, resistance training is the primary muscle-retention signal — full-body coverage keeps every muscle above the minimum effective weekly dose while circuit density raises session energy cost. Fat loss itself is driven by the diet-side deficit; training's job is protecting lean mass and adding expenditure, which this format does time-efficiently.
evidence: Five to nine hard sets a week per muscle is the minimum effective band
Lifting during a calorie deficit is what keeps the weight lost from being muscle
programs.expectedResults: With a sensible deficit and protein at ~1.6-2.2 g/kg: 0.5-1% bodyweight lost weekly with muscle largely preserved.
programs.cautions: Do not chase soreness; performance maintenance is the goal in a deficit.

programs.name: Hybrid Cut: Lift + Cardio Split
programs.whoIsItFor: Experienced-enough lifters cutting weight who refuse to lose strength and can give 4-5 hours a week.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Very high life stress or <7h sleep — combined stimulus needs recovery.
programs.schedule: Lift/cardio alternate; keep intervals 24h+ away from lower-body lifting.

progression.rule: Attempt to hold or slowly add lifting load through the cut; add one interval or 5 cardio minutes every 2 weeks.
progression.deload: Week 6: skip intervals, halve lifting sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Separating strength and cardio onto different days minimizes the interference effect on strength adaptations while the added aerobic work enlarges the weekly deficit. Heavy low-rep work in a cut is the strongest retention signal for both strength and mass.
evidence: Cardio and lifting interfere most when hard sessions sit on top of each other
Training with enough protein preserves lean mass while fat comes off
programs.expectedResults: Fat loss with strength held within ~5% of baseline for most.
programs.cautions: If lifts drop >10%, the deficit is too aggressive.

programs.name: Lower-Body Emphasis Sculpt

audience.note: Marketed to women, physiologically valid for anyone prioritizing lower-body development.

programs.whoIsItFor: Trainees prioritizing glute and leg development with maintenance-level upper-body work.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with balanced-physique goals (upper volume here is deliberately minimal).
programs.schedule: Lower/upper alternating with at least one rest day mid-week.

progression.rule: Top of range on all sets -> add load; abduction/pump work progresses by reps then band tension.
progression.deload: Week 6 or on 2 stalled sessions: -30% sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Glutes receive ~16-20 weekly sets across three frequency exposures — the high end of the productive volume band — via a mix of hip-thrust (high glute activation at short muscle length) and squat/hinge patterns (long-length loading), a combination associated with more complete regional hypertrophy. Upper body held at ~6 weekly sets per pattern, enough to maintain.
evidence: The hip thrust loads the glutes in their shortened position better than squatting alone
12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band for growth
Training a muscle twice a week beats once for the same weekly volume
programs.expectedResults: Visible lower-body development in 10 weeks with upper body maintained.
programs.cautions: Lower-back pump on thrusts means bracing needs work — reduce load, re-learn.

programs.name: Classic 5-Day Body-Part Split

audience.note: Traditional bodybuilding style; valid for anyone who enjoys one-muscle-a-day training.

programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters who love annihilating one muscle group per session and reliably train 5 fixed days.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone who misses sessions often (a missed day = that muscle skipped for the week); beginners.
programs.schedule: Mon-Fri, weekends off.

progression.rule: Add load when the top of the rep range is reached on all sets of an exercise.
progression.deload: Every 8th week, halve sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Once-weekly frequency per muscle is hypertrophically viable when weekly per-muscle volume is matched — meta-analytic evidence shows volume, more than frequency, drives growth. The format trades the small frequency advantage for very high per-session focus and simple adherence, which for lifters who love it is the deciding real-world variable.
evidence: Once weekly volume is matched, how it is split across days matters far less
Once weekly volume is equal, spreading it over more days changes little for growth
12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band for growth
programs.expectedResults: Comparable growth to higher-frequency splits at matched volume, given consistent attendance.
programs.cautions: Missed days don't get made up — consistency is the whole bet.

programs.name: Run Start: 0 to 5K
programs.whoIsItFor: Non-runners who want to run 5K continuously in ~9 weeks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Acute lower-limb injuries; significant cardiovascular conditions without medical clearance; consider brisk-walk progression first at BMI 35+.

weeklyStructure.session: 3min jog, 90s walk, 5min jog, 2.5min walk, 3min jog, 90s walk, 5min jog

programs.schedule: 3 non-consecutive days; every session starts with a 5-min brisk-walk warmup.

progression.rule: Only advance a week when all three sessions felt manageable; repeating a week is normal and expected.
progression.deload: Repeat any week on demand.

programs.scienceRationale: Walk-run interval progression builds aerobic capacity while capping impact exposure, the main driver of beginner running injuries — tissue tolerance (tendon, bone) adapts slower than cardiovascular fitness, so mileage ramps conservatively. Conversational intensity keeps sessions in the moderate domain where adherence and adaptation are both high.
evidence: A walk-run progression gets beginners running with far fewer injuries
Established aerobic progression guidelines
programs.expectedResults: Run 5K without stopping by week 9-11 (repeats included).
programs.cautions: Sharp localized pain (shin, knee, achilles) = stop and regress a week, don't push through.

programs.name: Move Free: Daily Mobility & Flexibility
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone stiff from desk work or lifting who wants measurably better range of motion in 15 min/day.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Hypermobility spectrum (needs strengthening, not more range); acute disc symptoms for the flexion drills.
programs.schedule: 6 days, ~15 min; pairs well as an evening routine or post-lift cooldown.

progression.rule: Weeks 1-2 as written; weeks 3-4 extend static holds to 60s and add gentle end-range contractions (5s push at 20% effort) to key stretches.
progression.deload: None needed at this intensity.

programs.scienceRationale: Meaningful range-of-motion gains require consistent near-daily exposure — total weekly stretch time matters more than any single session — and static holds of 30-60s at mild-moderate intensity are the best-evidenced dose. Adding light end-range isometrics (PNF-style) accelerates gains and builds usable strength in the new range.
evidence: Range of motion follows total weekly stretching time more than the length of any one session
Contract-relax stretching gains range of motion faster than holding a stretch alone
programs.expectedResults: Noticeably deeper squat, better overhead reach, and reduced desk stiffness within 4 weeks.
programs.cautions: Stretch to mild-moderate tension, never sharp pain or numbness/tingling.

programs.name: Rebuild: Graded Return to Training
programs.whoIsItFor: People CLEARED BY A CLINICIAN returning after injury or a long medical layoff who need a structured, conservative ramp — not a rehab protocol.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone not yet discharged from physiotherapy or without medical clearance; anyone with pain during daily activities. This program does not treat injuries.
programs.medicalDisclaimer: REQUIRED READING: This is general reconditioning after clearance, not rehabilitation. Follow your clinician's restrictions over anything written here.

slots.intensity: RPE 5-6 wk1-2, RPE 7 wk3-4, RPE 8 wk5-6

programs.schedule: 3 non-consecutive days; add sets (2->3) before load, load before intensity.

progression.rule: 24-hour rule: if symptoms increase for more than 24h after a session, repeat the previous week's dose. Progress volume first, then load, never both at once.
progression.deload: Any symptom flare = drop back one week.

programs.scienceRationale: Graded exposure with generous rep ranges and machine-first choices rebuilds tissue tolerance and confidence while capping spinal and joint shear. The volume-before-load rule and 24-hour symptom gate mirror standard progressive-loading principles used in late-stage rehab literature, applied conservatively for the post-discharge gap most gym programs ignore.
evidence: Graded, progressive loading is what rebuilds tolerance after a layoff
Loading through mild pain is safe when it is monitored against a clear rule
programs.expectedResults: Restored baseline work capacity and readiness to enter a normal beginner/novice program by week 7.
programs.cautions: This program is subordinate to clinical advice in every case of conflict.

programs.name: Strong for Life: 55+ Functional Strength
programs.whoIsItFor: Older adults who want strength, balance, and independence with two manageable weekly sessions.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Unmanaged cardiovascular conditions without clearance; severe osteoporosis needs clinician-guided loading.
programs.schedule: 2 sessions with 2-3 days between; daily walking encouraged.

progression.rule: Add reps to 12, then increase load by the smallest available increment. Balance drills progress by reducing support, then closing eyes.
progression.deload: Any week feeling run-down: same movements at half the sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Resistance training in older adults counters sarcopenia, preserves bone mineral density, and combined strength-plus-balance work is among the best-evidenced interventions for fall risk reduction. Two quality sessions capture the large majority of the dose-response benefit at an adherence-friendly commitment; power through the sit-to-stand and step-up patterns preserves the fast-twitch capacity that declines steepest with age.
evidence: Resistance training is the primary defence against age-related muscle loss
Balance and strength training together are what prevent falls
Even in the ninth decade, progressive resistance training builds strength and independence
programs.expectedResults: Easier stairs, chairs, and carrying within 6-8 weeks; measurable strength gains through week 12.
programs.cautions: Breathe continuously through reps (no breath-holding/Valsalva with blood pressure concerns).

programs.name: No-Gym Bodyweight Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone training at home with zero equipment who still wants real muscle and strength.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Advanced lifters chasing maximal load-based strength (progression ceiling without equipment).

slots.variant: single-leg hip hinge / sliding leg curl

programs.schedule: A/B/A then B/A/B, non-consecutive days.

progression.rule: When the top of a rep range is reached, move to the harder exercise variant instead of adding reps forever; a loaded backpack substitutes for added weight on squats/lunges.
progression.deload: Week 5: 2 sets per slot.

programs.scienceRationale: Hypertrophy at low external loads is achievable when sets approach failure — light-load training to near-failure produces growth comparable to heavy loads. Because bodyweight reps inflate quickly, progression here is mechanical (harder leverage variants) rather than purely rep-based, keeping sets in an effective proximity-to-failure zone.
evidence: Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when the effort matches
How close a set comes to failure is what determines its stimulus
programs.expectedResults: Visible muscle and big rep-strength gains in 8 weeks with zero equipment.
programs.cautions: Rows are the weak link at home — a sturdy table or bands are worth securing for back balance.

programs.name: 10K Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: Runners who own the 5K and want to complete (or race) a 10K in 8 weeks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with current running-related pain; true beginners (do Run Start: 0 to 5K first).

slots.reps: 10 min easy + 15-20 min comfortably hard + 10 min easy
starts 45 min wk1, +10 min every 2 wks, peaks 75-80 min wk7, 50 min wk8 (taper)

programs.schedule: Quality day never adjacent to long run; ~80% of weekly minutes stay easy.

progression.rule: Weekly minutes rise ~10%; every 4th week drops ~25% (built into wk4), taper in wk8.
progression.deload: Week 4 and race-week taper.

programs.scienceRationale: Polarized-leaning distribution (mostly easy, one weekly threshold session) reflects the best-evidenced intensity split for developing aerobic capacity while containing injury risk, which in runners tracks with rapid mileage spikes. Strides add neuromuscular speed at negligible fatigue cost.
evidence: Endurance athletes progress fastest on mostly-easy work with a small hard fraction
Running injuries track sudden jumps in weekly volume more than volume itself
programs.expectedResults: Complete 10K comfortably; typical novices race it at close to their 5K pace + 15-25 s/km.
programs.cautions: Persistent localized pain -> replace one run with cycling for a week.

programs.name: 5K Sharpener
programs.whoIsItFor: Runners chasing a 5K personal best in 6 weeks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Runners under 6 months of consistent base; interval work on an unprepared base is the classic injury recipe.

slots.reps: 3 min @ ~current 5K pace, 2 min jog between (wk1) -> 6 x 3 min slightly faster by wk5

programs.schedule: Hard days (intervals, tempo) separated by at least one easy/rest day. Week 6: halve interval volume, race weekend.

progression.rule: Hold paces, add one interval rep every 2 weeks; final week taper.
progression.deload: Race-week taper built in.

programs.scienceRationale: 5K performance is dominated by VO2max and running economy; interval bouts of ~3 minutes near VO2max pace are the classic highest-leverage stimulus, while the tempo session raises lactate threshold and easy volume maintains the aerobic floor.
evidence: Intervals at the pace that maximises oxygen uptake drive aerobic gains fastest
Roughly 80% easy and 20% hard beats training everything in the middle
programs.expectedResults: Typical 30-90 s 5K improvement for an intermediate over 6 weeks.
programs.cautions: Intervals feel productive — resist adding a third hard day; that's how shins break.

programs.name: FTP Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: Cyclists (indoor or outdoor) who want measurably higher sustainable power in 8 weeks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Brand-new riders (build 4-6 weeks of easy riding first).

slots.reps: 10 min @ 88-93% FTP (wk1) building to 3 x 15 min (wk6)
12 min @ 95-100% FTP building to 2 x 20 min

programs.schedule: Test FTP (20-min test x 0.95) in week 1 and week 8. Interval days separated by endurance days.

progression.rule: Extend interval duration before raising target percentage; retest FTP week 8 and reset zones.
progression.deload: Week 4: endurance rides only.

programs.scienceRationale: Sustainable power tracks lactate threshold, which responds strongly to accumulated time in the sweet-spot/threshold band; the surrounding zone-2 volume drives the mitochondrial and capillary adaptations underpinning it. Time-at-intensity progression raises training load without the injury/burnout profile of constant intensity increases.
evidence: Endurance improves most on mostly-easy work with a small hard fraction
Sustained work just below threshold gives the best return per hour on the bike
programs.expectedResults: 5-12% FTP improvement is typical for non-veterans over 8 weeks.
programs.cautions: Fuel interval days; under-eating around threshold work wrecks quality.

programs.name: Swim Smooth & Far
programs.whoIsItFor: Swimmers who want to go from surviving laps to swimming 1500m+ comfortably.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Non-swimmers (get stroke lessons first — technique coaching beats any program at that stage).
programs.schedule: 3 swims, any spacing; drills always precede the main set while fresh.

progression.rule: Repeat distance grows (100 -> 200 -> 400) while total volume rises gently; rest intervals stay fixed.
progression.deload: Week 4: technique day twice, no interval day.

programs.scienceRationale: In swimming, drag reduction (technique) outweighs fitness for novices — energy cost differences between swimmers are dominated by technique — so a third of all training time stays on drills. Interval lengthening builds continuous-swim capacity in controlled steps, and short sprints maintain feel-for-water and stroke power.
evidence: In front crawl, efficiency through the water beats raw power
Swim distance is built by turning intervals into continuous swimming
programs.expectedResults: Comfortable 1500m continuous swim by week 8 with a visibly longer stroke.
programs.cautions: Shoulder niggles = check catch mechanics early; swimmer's shoulder starts as a technique fault.

programs.name: Pitch Power: Football S&C
programs.whoIsItFor: Football (soccer) players adding 2-3 gym/field sessions around team practice for speed, repeat-sprint ability, and injury resilience.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: In-season players already training 5+ team sessions weekly should run only Day 1 (strength) of this plan.

slots.variant: nordic curl or slider leg curl

slots.reps: 6 x 30m shuttle, 20s between reps, 3 min between sets

programs.schedule: Never sprint the day after strength; keep 48h between Day 1 and Day 2 where possible. In-season: Day 1 only, 24-48h after match.

progression.rule: Strength: add load at RPE cap. Sprints: progress distance 20 -> 30m before adding reps. Nordics: progress range before reps.
progression.deload: Week 4: halve field volumes, keep intensity.

programs.scienceRationale: Hamstring eccentric strength work (nordic pattern) roughly halves hamstring injury risk in football, adductor/Copenhagen work targets the sport's other signature injury, and maximal-velocity sprint exposure both improves speed and acts as a vaccine against sprint-related strains. Repeat-sprint shuttles mirror the sport's demand profile better than steady cardio.
evidence: Nordic hamstring curls roughly halve hamstring injury rates
A simple adductor-strengthening protocol substantially reduces groin injuries
Regular exposure to high-speed running is what protects the hamstrings
programs.expectedResults: Faster 20m times, later-game legs, and materially lower soft-tissue injury risk.
programs.cautions: Nordics cause savage soreness at first — start with 2 sets of 4.

programs.name: Above the Rim: Basketball Athleticism
programs.whoIsItFor: Basketball players who want a higher vertical, quicker first step, and ankles/knees that survive the season.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Current patellar tendon pain — jumping volume here will aggravate it; resolve first.
programs.schedule: 48h between the two jump-heavy days; count team practices as jump volume and trim plyos in heavy practice weeks.

progression.rule: Strength lifts progress by load; plyos progress by variation difficulty (never volume beyond ~40 quality contacts/session).
progression.deload: Week 4: no depth work, half sprint volume.

programs.scienceRationale: Vertical jump improves most from combining heavy strength work with high-intent plyometrics — the mix outperforms either alone. Slow heavy tempo work builds patellar tendon capacity (the sport's chronic weak point), and deliberate landing mechanics training reduces knee injury risk, particularly relevant for female athletes given documented higher risk profiles.
evidence: Combining strength work with jump training raises vertical jump more than either alone
Tendons remodel under heavy, slow, progressive load
Coaching a controlled landing is what protects the knee
programs.expectedResults: 5-10cm vertical improvement over 8 weeks is common alongside a sharper first step.
programs.cautions: Quality over quantity on every jump — tired plyos are worthless and risky.

programs.name: Ring Ready: Boxing S&C
programs.whoIsItFor: Boxers adding structured strength and conditioning around bag/pad/sparring work.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Fight week (taper instead); anyone using this as a substitute for actual boxing training.

slots.reps: 3 min hard / 1 min easy (mimics round structure)

programs.schedule: Slot around boxing sessions: strength furthest from sparring; power day pairs well before technical (not sparring) sessions.

progression.rule: Strength by load; throws by intent and variation; engine by shaving the easy minute (1:00 -> 0:45) across weeks.
progression.deload: Week 4 and any fight week: -50% volume, keep some intent work.

programs.scienceRationale: Punching force is driven bottom-up — leg and trunk contributions dominate force generation in skilled punches — so lower-body max strength plus rotational med-ball power transfer directly. Round-structured intervals condition the exact work:rest signature of the ring, and 4-way neck isometrics build the musculature associated with better head-impact tolerance.
evidence: Most punching force comes from the legs and trunk, not the arm
Striking power comes from rate of force development, not maximal strength alone
A stronger neck reduces the head acceleration an impact produces
programs.expectedResults: Harder punching power markers, later-round freshness, sturdier neck and grip.
programs.cautions: Total weekly load includes sparring — cut here, never at boxing practice.

programs.name: Net Gains: Volleyball Performance
programs.whoIsItFor: Volleyball players wanting a bigger block/spike jump and a spike shoulder that lasts the season.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Active jumper's knee flare-ups (use the tendon-capacity day only until it settles).
programs.schedule: 48h between jump day and heavy lower day; match/practice jumps count toward weekly jump budget.

progression.rule: Lifts by load; jumps by variation and approach speed, capped ~40 contacts/session; cuff work by band tension.
progression.deload: Week 4: no plyos, tendon-tempo and cuff work only.

programs.scienceRationale: Spike-approach-specific jump training plus heavy strength is the highest-transfer combination for volleyball verticals, while jumper's knee — the sport's signature overuse issue — is managed proactively via heavy-slow tendon loading and a hard cap on weekly jump volume. Overhead athletes' shoulders depend on posterior cuff endurance and pull-dominant balance, addressed with the 2:1 pull bias.
evidence: Combining strength work with jump training raises vertical jump more than either alone
Jumper's knee is the volleyball player's occupational injury, and managing jump load prevents it
Heavy, slow loading is the treatment of choice for a stubborn patellar tendon
Overhead athletes need dedicated rotator-cuff and scapular conditioning
programs.expectedResults: Higher block/spike touch and a shoulder that tolerates full spiking loads.
programs.cautions: Never stack this jump day the day after a match.

programs.name: Court Speed: Racquet Athlete
programs.whoIsItFor: Tennis and padel players wanting quicker court movement, a heavier serve/smash, and elbow/shoulder durability.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Acute tennis elbow (start with the isometric protocol in the notes and reduced volume).

slots.variant: wrist extensor eccentric (Tyler twist or DB)

programs.schedule: Fit around match/practice days; power day pairs well the day before match play, never same-day before.

progression.rule: Throws progress by ball weight then speed; reactions by adding a decision cue; strength by load.
progression.deload: Week 4: halve throws and sprints.

programs.scienceRationale: Groundstroke and serve power are kinetic-chain products — hip/trunk rotation contributes the major share of racquet-head speed — so med-ball rotational work in sport-specific patterns is the highest-transfer power tool. Court movement is dominated by 1-4m lateral first steps, trained here reactively. Wrist-extensor eccentrics and posterior cuff endurance target the sport's two overuse hot spots.
evidence: The serve is a kinetic chain — force starts at the ground and arrives at the racket
Tennis is repeated short sprints and direction changes, and training should mirror that
Eccentric wrist-extensor work resolves tennis elbow
programs.expectedResults: Noticeably quicker to wide balls, heavier serve, resilient elbow/shoulder through the season.
programs.cautions: Racquet sports are one-side dominant — do all rotational work both directions.

programs.name: All-Round Athlete GPP
programs.whoIsItFor: Multi-sport or recreational athletes, or anyone whose sport isn't listed, wanting an all-quality athletic base: strong, fast, springy, conditioned.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Athletes in a dedicated competition block (use a sport-specific plan).
programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days; sprints and jumps always first, always fresh.

progression.rule: Lifts by load; sprints by distance then reps; intervals by shaving recovery.
progression.deload: Week 4: strength only, half sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Concurrent development of strength, speed, power, and both energy systems is manageable at 3 days when high-neural work (sprints, jumps) leads sessions fresh and interference is contained by day separation. This GPP breadth is the standard base layer under any later specialization.
evidence: Running and lifting interfere when stacked carelessly; separating and sequencing them manages it
A general preparation phase builds the base that later specific work is spent from
programs.expectedResults: Simultaneous improvements in sprint, jump, lifts, and conditioning for non-specialized athletes.
programs.cautions: This is a base — deep in-season sport demands should replace, not stack on, this plan.

programs.name: Trail Legs: Hiking & Trekking Prep
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone preparing for serious day hikes, trekking trips, or mountain holidays who wants legs and lungs that outlast the trail.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Acute knee/ankle injuries; those with cardiac conditions need clearance for loaded climbing work.

slots.variant: incline treadmill walk or stairs or hill repeats, loaded pack
slots.reps: wk1: 25 min w/ 5kg -> wk8: 45 min w/ 10-12kg

slots.variant: long walk/hike, rolling terrain if possible
slots.reps: wk1: 75 min -> wk8: 3h (light pack from wk4)

programs.schedule: Long day on the weekend; 48h between strength and loaded climb.

progression.rule: Pack weight rises before duration; step-down eccentrics progress by box height.
progression.deload: Week 5: no pack anywhere, shorter long day.

programs.scienceRationale: Trekking capacity is uphill aerobic work plus eccentric quad tolerance for descents — the under-trained half that causes most post-hike wreckage — so slow step-downs deliberately precondition eccentric load (repeated-bout effect). Progressive pack loading and single-leg balance work address the load-carriage and ankle-sprain realities of uneven terrain.
evidence: The first hard session is the sorest — one exposure protects against the next
Carrying load well is a trainable adaptation, not just raw strength
programs.expectedResults: Comfortable 5-7h mountain days with a loaded pack and quads that work the day after.
programs.cautions: Break in the actual boots on the long days — the program can't fix blisters.

programs.name: Long Drive: Golf Rotational Power
programs.whoIsItFor: Golfers who want more clubhead speed and a back that tolerates a full season of swings.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Acute low-back episodes (settle first; the rotation volume here is meaningful).

slots.variant: med-ball rotational scoop throw (swing pattern, both sides)

programs.schedule: Power day 48h+ before competitive rounds; mobility day anytime, ideal on golf days.

progression.rule: Throws by ball weight then velocity intent; mobility by achieved range; strength by load.
progression.deload: Week 4: mobility + light strength only.

programs.scienceRationale: Clubhead speed correlates strongly with rotational power output and thoracic/hip rotation range — the X-factor stretch depends on hip-shoulder separation, trained here via loaded chops, high-intent throws in the swing pattern, and targeted thoracic/hip-IR mobility. Bilateral throw work and anti-rotation strength protect the lead-side low back, golf's most common complaint.
evidence: Leg and trunk strength and power are the physical determinants of golf performance
Golf-specific conditioning raises club-head speed
Separating hip and shoulder rotation is what generates club-head speed
programs.expectedResults: 3-8 mph clubhead speed gains commonly reported from 8-week rotational programs; easier full turn.
programs.cautions: Throw both directions every session — one-sided rotation is how golf backs break.

programs.name: Push / Pull / Legs (3-Day)
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters who love the PPL structure but only have 3 days.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone chasing maximum growth rate with 5-6 days available (each muscle trains only 1x/week here).
programs.schedule: Any 3 non-consecutive days.

progression.rule: Top of rep range on all sets -> add load next session.
progression.deload: Week 6: halve sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Once-weekly frequency per muscle grows muscle effectively when weekly volume is sufficient — meta-analytic evidence shows frequency matters little at matched volume — and ~12-16 sets per function per week lands in the productive band. The trade is a slightly lower ceiling than higher frequencies for a structure many lifters simply enjoy and stick to, and adherence beats optimization.
evidence: Once weekly volume is matched, how it is split across days matters far less
12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band for growth
programs.expectedResults: Steady hypertrophy and strength gains at a very sustainable schedule.
programs.cautions: Don't turn each day into a 2-hour marathon — the listed volume is the productive part.

programs.name: Powerbuilding: Strong & Built
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters who refuse to choose between big lifts and a big physique.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Beginners (a simple linear program progresses both faster at that stage).
programs.schedule: 4 days, heavy lift first each day while fresh.

progression.rule: Main lifts: add load when top set hits 5 reps @ RPE 8 (weekly-ish). Accessories: double progression in-range.
progression.deload: Every 5th week: main lifts -15% load, accessories half sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Low-rep top sets develop maximal strength via specificity while backoff and accessory volume supplies the 10+ weekly sets per muscle that drive hypertrophy — the two adaptations coexist happily when intensity and volume are assigned to separate slots rather than blended. Strength gains show pronounced diminishing returns from extra volume, so the heavy work stays minimal-effective.
evidence: Strength plateaus with added volume sooner than growth does
Weekly hard sets and muscle growth rise together
programs.expectedResults: PRs on the big four alongside visible muscle gain over 10 weeks.
programs.cautions: The top-set RPE 8 cap is the program — grinding RPE 10 singles wrecks the week.

programs.name: Minimum Effective Dose: 2-Day Strength
programs.whoIsItFor: Busy people (new parents, crunch periods, shift workers) who can genuinely commit to only 2 sessions.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody, really — but expectations must match the dose: this maintains and slowly builds, it doesn't maximize.
programs.schedule: 2 sessions, 2-4 days apart; walk on other days if possible.

progression.rule: Top of range on all sets -> add load. Slow is fine; consistency is the mechanism.
progression.deload: Only when needed: same weights, 2 sets.

programs.scienceRationale: The first weekly sets deliver a disproportionate share of total possible gains — dose-response curves rise steeply then flatten — so ~6 hard sets per pattern per week captures a large fraction of the benefit at a fraction of the time. For strength and health outcomes, low-dose resistance training is dramatically better than none, and a plan that survives a busy life beats an optimal plan that doesn't.
evidence: The first few hard sets per muscle do most of the work; each one after adds less
Even under five hard sets a week still produces real growth
As little as 30-60 minutes of lifting a week improves long-term health outcomes
programs.expectedResults: Real strength progress and maintained/slowly growing muscle on 90 min/week.
programs.cautions: Every set counts at this dose — no phoned-in sessions.

programs.name: Dumbbell Department: Home DB Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: Home trainees with only dumbbells (ideally adjustable) and maybe a bench.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone whose heaviest dumbbell is already easy for 20+ reps on lower-body work — progression will stall without heavier bells.

slots.variant: incline or deficit pushup + DB fly

programs.schedule: Upper/Lower alternating, e.g. Mon/Tue/Thu/Fri.

progression.rule: Top of range -> add load; when load jumps are too big (fixed DBs), switch to the single-limb variant to double effective intensity.
progression.deload: Week 6: half sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Dumbbells cover every movement pattern, and unilateral variants solve the classic home problem of coarse load jumps by doubling the load per limb without new equipment. Higher rep ranges near failure produce equivalent hypertrophy to heavier loads, which is exactly the adaptation lever when maximum load is capped.
evidence: Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when the effort matches
Single-limb work exposes and corrects side-to-side imbalances
programs.expectedResults: Full-body muscle growth rivaling gym training up to the point your dumbbells run out.
programs.cautions: Adjustable dumbbells to at least 24-32kg are the difference between 10 weeks and a year of usefulness.

programs.name: Volume-Intensity Wave: Intermediate 3-Day
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters who just stalled on session-to-session linear progression and want classic weekly progression (Texas-method-style structure).
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Beginners still adding weight every session; advanced lifters (weekly PRs eventually stall too).
programs.schedule: Mon (volume) / Wed (recovery) / Fri (intensity) or equivalent spacing.

progression.rule: Friday sets a weekly 5RM PR; Monday's volume recalculates from it. Two failed Fridays on a lift -> drop that lift's Friday weight 5% and switch its rep target to 3s for the next cycle.
progression.deload: On double-failure, per lift.

programs.scienceRationale: The volume-day stress / recovery-day maintenance / intensity-day expression structure operationalizes the fitness-fatigue model at a weekly cadence — appropriate when adaptation slows past the novice stage. High-specificity heavy fives with big rests target maximal strength while total weekly volume stays in the moderate band that strength (unlike hypertrophy) responds to efficiently.
evidence: Performance is fitness minus fatigue, so fatigue is managed rather than merely accumulated
For strength, frequency keeps helping while added volume plateaus early
Multi-joint strength takes off once a muscle gets at least six hard sets a week
programs.expectedResults: Weekly PRs for 8-16 weeks — a typical full intermediate cycle — adding 10-25kg to squat 5RM.
programs.cautions: Volume day is brutally hard done honestly; don't add accessories on top.

programs.name: Bodyweight Skills: Pull-up, Dip, Handstand

audience.prerequisite: Can do 10 pushups and hang from a bar 20s

programs.whoIsItFor: Trainees who want gymnastic-style upper-body skills: clean pull-ups, deep dips, and a freestanding handstand journey.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Wrist or shoulder issues that don't tolerate loaded end-range positions yet.

slots.variant: handstand progression: wall hold -> chest-to-wall -> toe pulls
dip progression: support hold -> negatives -> full

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days; handstand work always first while nervous system is fresh.

progression.rule: Advance to the next exercise variant when the current one hits target reps/time with 2 in reserve and clean form; skill work (handstand) progresses by hold time then wall distance.
progression.deload: Week 6: skill work only, no strength sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Strength-skill hybrids respond best to frequent, submaximal, high-quality practice — motor learning improves with distributed practice at low fatigue — so skills lead sessions fresh and strength sets keep reps in reserve. Mechanical progression ladders (harder leverages) function as bodyweight's loading mechanism, keeping intensity in the strength zone.
evidence: Skill is built by frequent, spaced practice rather than long occasional sessions
Strength does not require training to failure — getting close is enough
Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure
programs.expectedResults: Typical 12-week outcomes from the stated baseline: 5-10 clean pull-ups, solid dips, 60s chest-to-wall handstand.
programs.cautions: Wrists adapt slower than muscles — never skip the prep work.

programs.name: Peak Week Prep: Powerlifting Taper Block

audience.prerequisite: Established recent training maxes; several months of consistent training

programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters 6 weeks out from a meet or a planned 1RM test day.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone without a base block behind them — peaking expresses fitness, it doesn't create it.

weeklyStructure.focus: test/meet week: openers only early week, then compete/test

programs.schedule: Squat and deadlift days separated by 72h; all accessories stripped from week 4.

progression.rule: Intensity climbs weekly as volume falls; week 5 taper cuts volume ~50% while keeping bar speed work; openers = a weight you can triple on your worst day.
progression.deload: The taper IS the deload.

programs.scienceRationale: Peaking exploits the fitness-fatigue model: heavy specific practice raises preparedness while the pre-test volume taper sheds accumulated fatigue faster than fitness decays, producing peak expressed strength on the day. Taper research consistently shows performance gains from ~40-60% volume reductions over 1-2 weeks with intensity maintained.
evidence: A planned taper before a test raises performance on the day
Cutting volume while holding intensity sharpens strength for a test
Performance is fitness minus fatigue, so fatigue is managed rather than merely accumulated
programs.expectedResults: Well-executed peaks typically express 2-5% above training-cycle projections.
programs.cautions: The most common peaking error is testing PRs in week 3-4 — the PR belongs on test day only.

programs.name: Arm Day, Every Day-ish: Arm Specialization
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters whose arms lag the rest of their physique and who accept maintenance elsewhere for 8 weeks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with elbow tendon grumbles (this volume will find them); beginners (everything grows on normal programs).
programs.schedule: 48h between the two arm-primary days.

progression.rule: In-range progression; long-length movements progress first priority.
progression.deload: Week 5: arm volume halved — elbows will tell you anyway.

programs.scienceRationale: Specialization concentrates volume where growth is wanted: arms receive ~20+ direct weekly sets (upper end of the productive band, plus indirect work) while other muscles hold at maintenance doses, which preserve size at a fraction of building volume. Long-muscle-length loading (incline curls, overhead extensions) is emphasized per emerging evidence of superior lengthened-position hypertrophy.
evidence: Smaller muscles like the triceps reward the higher end of the volume band
Keeping muscle takes roughly a third of the volume it took to build it
Training a muscle in its stretched position produces more growth per set
programs.expectedResults: Measurable arm circumference gains (0.5-1.5cm) in 8 weeks for intermediates.
programs.cautions: Elbow tendons adapt slower than biceps — the RPE 9 cap is load management, respect it.

programs.name: V-Taper: Upper-Body Emphasis

audience.note: Classic aesthetics emphasis; valid for anyone prioritizing shoulders/back/chest.

programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters chasing the wide-shoulder, wide-back, tight-waist look, with legs at maintenance.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with balanced goals — leg volume here is deliberately minimal.
programs.schedule: Any order with one rest day mid-week; back and shoulder days not adjacent if possible.

progression.rule: In-range progression; lateral raises progress by reps before load (form decays fast with load).
progression.deload: Week 6: half sets everywhere.

programs.scienceRationale: The visual V is lat width plus delt cap over a stable waist, so lats and side delts get 16-20 weekly sets at the top of the productive band while legs hold at the well-evidenced maintenance dose (roughly a third of building volume preserves size). Rear-delt volume is high because the posterior shoulder both completes the cap and balances all the pressing.
evidence: 12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band for growth
Keeping muscle takes roughly a third of the volume it took to build it
Training a muscle twice a week beats once for the same weekly volume
programs.expectedResults: Visibly wider frame in 10 weeks; strength up on presses and pulls.
programs.cautions: Legs at maintenance is a temporary emphasis, not a lifestyle.

programs.name: Full-Body High-Frequency Growth
programs.whoIsItFor: Lifters who prefer hitting everything every session and leaving the gym in under an hour, 3x weekly.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Lifters who like body-part focus days (this is the opposite philosophy).
programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days.

progression.rule: In-range progression per exercise; different bias each day means no two sessions compete for the same recovery.
progression.deload: Week 6: 2 sets per slot.

programs.scienceRationale: Distributing 9-12 weekly sets per pattern across three exposures keeps every set high-quality (first sets of a session outperform the sixth), and thrice-weekly muscle protein synthesis stimulation suits the 24-48h MPS window. Per-session volume stays low enough that sessions end inside an hour with intensity intact.
evidence: Training a muscle twice a week beats once for the same weekly volume
Muscle stays primed to grow for roughly two days after a session
12-20 hard sets per muscle per week is the productive band for growth
programs.expectedResults: Growth comparable to splits at equal volume, with shorter, fresher sessions.
programs.cautions: Every session touches legs — manage soreness expectations in week 1-2.

programs.name: Pull-Up Project: 0 to 10 Reps
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone from zero pull-ups to a shaky few who wants a strict set of 10. Especially effective for women, for whom the first pull-up is a common and beatable barrier.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Current shoulder impingement symptoms in overhead positions.

slots.variant: hardest available: negatives (5s down) or band-assisted or full
easy singles/doubles spread through the session
band face pull or rear fly

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive; test max reps end of week 4 and week 8 only.

progression.rule: Reduce band assistance (or lengthen negatives) when strength-day sets hit 5 clean reps; volume day always stays 2+ from failure.
progression.deload: Week 5: volume day only, twice.

programs.scienceRationale: The pull-up responds to high practice frequency at low fatigue — the grease-the-groove principle — combined with eccentric-emphasized strength work, since eccentric capacity precedes concentric in movements you can't yet perform. Submaximal volume builds the lat/arm tissue while avoiding the failure-chasing that stalls most pull-up attempts.
evidence: You can lower more than you can lift, and training the lowering builds the lift
Practice spread across more days beats the same practice crammed into fewer
Stopping a rep or two short preserves the quality of every set that follows
programs.expectedResults: From 0: first strict rep by week 4-6, 3-6 by week 8. From 3: typically 8-10 by week 8.
programs.cautions: Full range every rep — chin over bar, full hang — or the reps you count won't count.

programs.name: Farm Strong: Carries & Functional Strength
programs.whoIsItFor: People who want strength that shows up in life — carrying, lifting awkward things, grip that doesn't quit — with a strongman-lite flavor.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Uncontrolled hypertension (loaded carries spike blood pressure); hernia history without clearance.
programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days; carries always after the main lift, never before.

progression.rule: Carries progress load at fixed distance, then distance at fixed load, alternating cycles; lifts by double progression.
progression.deload: Week 6: no carries, lifts at half sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Loaded carries train trunk stiffness, grip, and hip stability under moving load — qualities strongly tied to real-world function and low transferable injury risk — while the hinge/squat/press/pull base supplies conventional strength. Grip strength itself is a notable longitudinal marker of health outcomes, and carries are its most scalable trainer.
evidence: Loaded carries build the trunk stiffness that transfers to every other lift
Grip strength is one of the strongest simple predictors of long-term health
Strongman events build strength in awkward, real-world positions
programs.expectedResults: Grip, trunk, and everyday-strength gains that show up outside the gym within 6-8 weeks.
programs.cautions: Set the weights down with a hinge, not a drop-and-dodge.

programs.name: One Bell: Kettlebell Strength & Engine

audience.prerequisite: Competent hip hinge; learn the swing pattern first (a session with a coach or careful video study)

programs.whoIsItFor: People with one or two kettlebells who want strength, conditioning, and fat loss from a single tool.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone who hasn't learned the swing — a bad swing is a low-back complaint generator.

slots.variant: single-arm front-rack hold or TGU practice
complex: 6 swings -> 4 cleans -> 2 presses per side, unbroken

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days; the EMOM swing day is the conditioning centerpiece.

progression.rule: EMOM progresses 10 -> 15 min before adding swing reps; strength moves progress reps then bell size (KB jumps are big — use rep buffer).
progression.deload: Week 5: strength day only, twice.

programs.scienceRationale: Ballistic hip-hinge work (swings) trains posterior-chain power and elevates heart rate into productive conditioning zones simultaneously — kettlebell interval protocols produce meaningful VO2 and strength adaptations in the same sessions. Single-arm loading adds anti-rotation trunk demand to every rep, buying core training for free.
evidence: The kettlebell swing carries a real cardiovascular cost alongside its strength work
Swing training builds strength and power at the same time
Kettlebell work transfers to barbell strength
programs.expectedResults: Concurrent strength, conditioning, and body-comp improvements on ~2 hours/week.
programs.cautions: The swing is a hinge, not a squat, and the bell floats — never lift it with your arms.

programs.name: Engine Block: 4-Week HIIT Focus
programs.whoIsItFor: A short, sharp conditioning block for people who want a rapid fitness bump — as a standalone month or dropped between strength blocks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Cardiovascular conditions without clearance; complete beginners (build a steady-state base first).

slots.reps: 3 min hard / 3 min easy (wk1) -> 5 x 3 min (wk3)

programs.schedule: Hard/easy alternation strictly enforced; the two interval days never adjacent.

progression.rule: Add one interval rep or trim recovery each week per the day notes; week 4 short-interval day is the peak session.
progression.deload: None — the block is 4 weeks by design; deload the following week before the next block.

programs.scienceRationale: High-intensity interval training produces VO2max improvements comparable to or exceeding much longer moderate-intensity programs — the interval stimulus drives central cardiovascular adaptation time-efficiently — while the two easy days preserve the polarized distribution that keeps the hard days actually hard.
evidence: Short, hard intervals produce aerobic adaptations out of proportion to their time cost
Intervals raise aerobic capacity at least as much as steady work, in less time
Endurance improves most on mostly-easy work with a small hard fraction
programs.expectedResults: Measurable VO2/pace improvements inside 4 weeks; pairs well before or after a strength block.
programs.cautions: HIIT quality collapses if every day becomes hard — the easy days are load-bearing.

programs.name: Walk Strong: Foundations for Bigger Bodies

audience.note: Designed for heavier beginners and anyone for whom running or jumping is currently unpleasant or joint-hostile.

programs.whoIsItFor: Beginners carrying extra weight who want a realistic, joint-friendly on-ramp: walking as the engine, simple strength as the frame.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody by fitness level — but unmanaged cardiovascular/metabolic conditions need a doctor's go-ahead first.

slots.reps: wk1: 20 min -> +5 min every 2 wks -> wk11: 45 min; add gentle hills from wk6

slots.variant: hip hinge to wall -> band/DB RDL

programs.schedule: Walks and strength can share days if needed (walk after); nothing is ever done sore-to-limping.

progression.rule: Walking by duration then hills; strength by the variant ladder (wall -> incline -> floor), reps before variant. Progress only what felt easy.
progression.deload: Any week life happens: keep the walks, skip strength guilt-free.

programs.scienceRationale: Walking is the highest-adherence, lowest-injury exercise available and its energy cost scales with bodyweight, making it disproportionately effective for heavier individuals; step-count and walking-volume increases show robust dose-response relationships with health outcomes. The strength ladder preserves lean mass in the deficit and rebuilds joint confidence, and adherence-first design reflects the strongest predictor of long-term weight-management success: consistency, not intensity.
evidence: Daily steps track closely with long-term health, with most of the benefit well before 10,000
Training with enough protein preserves lean mass while fat comes off
Adherence, not the particular diet or split, is what predicts the result
programs.expectedResults: With a moderate calorie deficit: sustainable fat loss, visibly easier daily movement by week 6, real strength by week 12.
programs.cautions: Shoes matter more here than in any other plan — replace worn-out soles before week 1.

programs.name: Rebuild: Postnatal Return to Strength

audience.prerequisite: Cleared for exercise at postnatal checkup (typically 6+ weeks postpartum; longer after C-section per clinician)

programs.whoIsItFor: Mothers CLEARED BY THEIR CLINICIAN who want a structured, conservative return to training that respects core and pelvic-floor recovery.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone not yet cleared; anyone with unresolved pelvic-floor symptoms (leaking, heaviness, pain) — see a pelvic health physiotherapist first, this program is not a substitute.
programs.medicalDisclaimer: REQUIRED READING: Postnatal recovery varies enormously. Clinician clearance is a prerequisite, symptoms (pelvic pressure/heaviness, leaking, doming along the midline, pain) are a stop-and-regress signal, and a pelvic health physio consult is the gold standard first step where available.

slots.variant: diaphragmatic breathing + gentle pelvic floor engage/relax cycles

slots.intensity: no midline doming — regress if it appears
same ramp — extra back volume is deliberate (feeding/carrying posture)
comfortable — trains the carrying you're already doing all day

programs.schedule: 3 non-consecutive days; walking encouraged daily as tolerated. Impact work (running, jumping) is deliberately absent — reintroduce beyond week 8, ideally with pelvic-floor-informed guidance.

progression.rule: Progress only symptom-free: any pelvic heaviness, leaking, doming, or pain -> regress one step and hold a week. Volume before load, load before intensity.
progression.deload: Sleep-deprivation weeks (they'll happen): core day only is a complete session.

programs.scienceRationale: Postnatal tissue (abdominal wall, pelvic floor) remodels for months; graded, symptom-gated loading with breathing-led core re-engagement is the consensus approach across postnatal exercise guidance, and early resumption of moderate activity benefits both physical recovery and mood. Diastasis management favors progressive tension over avoidance, with midline doming as the regression cue.
evidence: Established postpartum return-to-exercise guidance
Progressive loading, not avoidance, is the consensus approach to abdominal separation
Postnatal return to running follows a staged progression gated on real criteria, not a calendar
Postnatal exercise measurably improves mood
programs.expectedResults: Restored core function and confidence, baseline strength, and readiness for normal beginner programming by week 9+.
programs.cautions: Symptoms outrank the plan, always. This program never competes with a pelvic health professional's advice.

programs.name: Upper Hand: Women's Upper-Body Strength

audience.note: Addresses the most common structural gap in women's training; physiologically valid for anyone with lagging upper-body strength.

programs.whoIsItFor: Women who've built lower-body strength but want pressing/pulling power and visible upper-body development to match — including that first pull-up.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone wanting lower-body emphasis (see Lower-Body Emphasis Sculpt — this is its mirror).
programs.schedule: Press/pull days separated by the lower day where possible.

progression.rule: Presses/rows by double progression; pull-up slot by assistance reduction (band down-grades) once 5 clean reps hit.
progression.deload: Week 6: half sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Women's relative strength gap versus men is concentrated in the upper body, which is precisely the argument for prioritized upper volume — muscle tissue responds to training equally by sex on a relative basis, and women often tolerate volume and recover between sets well. Upper-body work receives ~2x lower-body volume here while the lower maintenance dose preserves existing strength.
evidence: Men and women gain strength and muscle at the same relative rate
Keeping muscle takes roughly a third of the volume it took to build it
The strength gap between sexes is far wider in the upper body than the lower
programs.expectedResults: First strict pull-up (or several) for most within the 10 weeks; visible shoulder/back development; pressing PRs.
programs.cautions: The pull-up ladder rewards patience — assistance drops beat grinding failures.

programs.name: Prime Time: 40+ Recomposition
programs.whoIsItFor: Adults 40+ who want to lose fat and gain muscle simultaneously with joint-considerate programming and realistic recovery.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody by age — but existing joint issues should map to the substitution notes, and health conditions need clearance.

slots.variant: DB, neutral grip if shoulders prefer

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive; daily 7-10k steps is half the fat-loss engine. Protein target matters more at this age: ~1.6-2.2 g/kg.

progression.rule: In-range progression; joints vote — any movement that consistently aches gets swapped for its listed variant, no heroics.
progression.deload: Every 6th week: half sets, keep moving.

programs.scienceRationale: Body recomposition — simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain — is well-documented in untrained and returning adults including middle age, given sufficient protein and progressive resistance training. Anabolic resistance of aging is offset by slightly higher protein and consistent mechanical tension, and 8-12 rep moderate loads deliver the stimulus with lower joint stress than maximal work.
evidence: Gaining muscle while losing fat is achievable, especially earlier in training
Protein returns flatten out around 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight a day
Older muscle needs a bigger protein dose and a harder stimulus to respond
programs.expectedResults: Over 12 weeks: waist down, strength up, scale possibly unimpressed — the mirror and the belt tell the real story.
programs.cautions: Recovery is programming too now: sleep short-changed = one fewer set, not one more coffee.

programs.name: Machine Start: Gym Confidence Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: First-time gym-goers, the gym-anxious, and anyone who wants results while learning the room — machines only, no free-weight learning curve, minimal setup to get wrong.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody — this is the lowest-barrier entry in the library. Free-weight plans simply progress further later.

days.name: Full body (same each visit, alternating A/B emphasis)

slots.variant: seated leg curl (B days: leg extension instead)

programs.schedule: Same 6 machines every visit — familiarity is the design. Note seat/pin settings in the app after session 1.

progression.rule: Reach 15 clean reps on all sets -> next pin down. Simple on purpose.
progression.deload: Life weeks: 2 sets per machine still counts.

programs.scienceRationale: Machines produce comparable hypertrophy and strength to free weights when effort is matched, while removing balance and setup demands — which lowers the perceived-competence barrier that drives early gym dropout. A fixed, repeated routine builds self-efficacy, the strongest psychological predictor of exercise adherence in new exercisers.
evidence: Machines and free weights build strength and muscle comparably
Confidence built from small, repeatable wins is what sustains training
programs.expectedResults: Real strength and visible tone in 8 weeks — and a person who walks into the gym like they belong, because they do.
programs.cautions: Graduation path: after week 8, swap one machine per week for its free-weight cousin if desired.

programs.name: Glide Path: Low-Impact Lean-Out

audience.note: For joints that veto running and jumping: everything here is zero- or low-impact.

programs.whoIsItFor: People with cranky knees, hips, or ankles (or higher bodyweight) who want an effective fat-loss engine without impact.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Acute joint injuries still need clearance — low-impact is not no-load.

slots.variant: leg press or box squat (pain-free depth)

programs.schedule: Alternate strength and cardio days; daily easy walking as joints allow.

progression.rule: Strength by double progression; intervals add one round per fortnight; steady day +5 min weekly.
progression.deload: Week 5: strength days only.

programs.scienceRationale: Fat loss requires an energy deficit, not impact — cycling, swimming, and elliptical work produce equivalent cardiovascular and caloric outcomes to running at matched effort, minus the joint loading. The strength half preserves lean mass through the deficit, and pain-free strength work around sensitive joints typically improves rather than threatens them.
evidence: At matched intensity, any cardio modality delivers much the same aerobic benefit
Training with enough protein preserves lean mass while fat comes off
In knee osteoarthritis, progressive loading reduces pain — joints do better used than spared
programs.expectedResults: Steady fat loss with zero impact-related flare-ups; joints commonly feel better by week 8, not worse.
programs.cautions: "Pain-free depth" is a moving target that usually improves — chase it gradually.

programs.name: Solid Ground: Strength & Bone Through Menopause
programs.whoIsItFor: Women in perimenopause and beyond who want to counter the accelerated bone and muscle loss of this life stage with properly loaded training — not the gentle-toning myth.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Diagnosed osteoporosis with fracture history needs clinician-guided loading parameters first (this plan suits osteopenia-range and prevention).
programs.medicalDisclaimer: With diagnosed low bone density, share this plan with your clinician before starting; impact and loading progressions may need individual tailoring.

slots.variant: impact dose: 10 firm heel drops or low hops (wk5+, if joints allow)
single-leg balance ladder (support -> free -> eyes closed)

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days; the impact micro-dose rides on day A only.

progression.rule: Heavy lifts progress by load in the 5-8 range — the loading magnitude is what bone responds to; balance ladder progresses by support reduction.
progression.deload: Every 6th week: half sets, no impact.

programs.scienceRationale: Bone adapts to high-magnitude loading: heavy resistance training plus brief impact exposure improved bone density and stature outcomes in postmenopausal women with low bone mass in the LIFTMOR trial, overturning the light-weights convention. Estrogen decline also accelerates muscle and power loss; heavy lifting plus intentional fast concentric work addresses both, and balance work attacks the fall half of the fracture equation.
evidence: Heavy, supervised lifting improves bone density in postmenopausal women
Resistance training is the primary defence against age-related muscle loss
Balance work combined with strength training reduces falls
programs.expectedResults: Strength gains within weeks; bone adaptation is slower — the 12 weeks establish the loading habit that pays over years.
programs.cautions: Spinal flexion under load is the one pattern kept out — hinge with a set back, always.

programs.name: Mini-Cut: 6-Week Aggressive Lean Phase

audience.prerequisite: 1+ years consistent training; not appropriate coming off a previous diet phase

programs.whoIsItFor: Experienced lifters running a deliberate, short, aggressive fat-loss phase between building blocks — maximum retention stimulus, minimum junk volume.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone with disordered-eating history (short aggressive phases are a poor fit — a gentler plan serves better); beginners; anyone unable to keep protein high through it.
programs.schedule: Strictly 6 weeks then done — back to maintenance for at least as long as the cut. Daily steps 8-12k; protein 2.2-2.7 g/kg during the phase.

progression.rule: The goal is NOT progression — it's holding heavy loads while the deficit does its work. Any lift dropping >5% = eat slightly more, don't train harder.
progression.deload: The maintenance phase after IS the deload.

programs.scienceRationale: Short aggressive deficits in trained lifters preserve muscle when protein is very high and heavy mechanical tension is maintained — retention tracks with training intensity more than volume, so volume is trimmed and load defended. Hard-capping the phase at 6 weeks limits the adaptive fatigue and adherence decay that erode longer aggressive diets.
evidence: Very lean athletes need protein at the top of the range to hold on to muscle
Too steep an energy deficit blunts the adaptation the training is meant to buy
High protein plus hard training preserves — and can even add — muscle in a steep deficit
programs.expectedResults: Typically 3-5% bodyweight lost over 6 weeks with strength substantially intact.
programs.cautions: The end date is a feature — mini-cuts that become maxi-cuts surrender the muscle they were protecting.

programs.name: Express 30: Half-Hour Full-Body
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone whose realistic window is 30 minutes, door to door — lunch-break training, parents, shift workers.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody; expectations just scale to the dose.

days.name: Session A (paired sets: A1/A2 alternate, 60s between)

programs.schedule: A/B/A then B/A/B; pairing non-competing movements is what fits 22 hard sets/week into 90 total minutes.

progression.rule: In-range progression; if a session runs long, cut the finisher, never the pairs.
progression.deload: Skip weeks happen — the program forgives, just resume.

programs.scienceRationale: Paired (antagonist/non-competing) sets cut session time roughly in half with no strength or hypertrophy penalty versus traditional rest — recovery of one movement happens during the other's set. Total weekly hard sets stay above minimum-effective thresholds, and supersetting research shows equivalent adaptations at substantially reduced session duration.
evidence: Meaningful gains are available from short, well-structured sessions
Pairing non-competing exercises halves session time without costing results
There is a low but real minimum weekly dose that still grows muscle
programs.expectedResults: Comparable results to hour-long sessions at this volume tier — the limiting factor was never the clock.
programs.cautions: The 60s pair-rest is real rest — phone stays in the pocket or the math breaks.

programs.name: Hybrid Base: Run + Lift Concurrent
programs.whoIsItFor: The hybrid-athlete crowd: people who want to run well AND lift well and refuse to pick a side.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone peaking for a specific race or meet (concurrent training trades peaks for breadth).

slots.intensity: RPE 8 — tendon insurance for the running

slots.reps: tempo: 20 min comfortably hard / intervals: 5 x 3 min hard, 2 min jog

programs.schedule: The interference-management rules ARE the program: quality run never within 24h after lower strength; long run followed by a rest day; lower day earliest in the week.

progression.rule: Lifts by double progression; running by ~10% weekly minutes with week 4 down ~25%.
progression.deload: Week 4 running down-week; lifting deloads only if bar speed says so.

programs.scienceRationale: Concurrent training's interference effect is real but modest and largely manageable through scheduling — separating quality run stimulus from lower-body lifting by 24h+ preserves most strength adaptation, and the effect runs one direction (endurance blunts strength/power, not vice versa; lifting actively improves running economy). Calf loading doubles as achilles tendon protection against the added mileage.
evidence: Cardio and lifting interfere most when hard sessions sit on top of each other
Strength training improves running and cycling economy
Strength training improves distance-running performance without adding bulk
programs.expectedResults: Simultaneous progress on 5K pace and big-lift numbers — slower than specializing in either, better than either alone.
programs.cautions: Adding a sixth day is the classic hybrid mistake — the recovery day is what makes five work.

programs.name: Desk Reset: Posture & Pain-Proofing
programs.whoIsItFor: Desk workers with the classic pattern — tight chest and hips, grumpy neck and upper back, dormant glutes — who want to feel structurally human again.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Radiating pain, numbness, or tingling into arms/legs is a clinician matter first, not a program matter.

slots.intensity: RPE 8 — pulling is the theme of this whole program
RPE 8 — pushing earns its place, 2:1 pull bias overall

slots.variant: thoracic extension over roller + open book

programs.schedule: Plus the real prescription: a 2-minute movement snack every hour of sitting — stand, 10 squats or a hallway walk. The program fixes capacity; the snacks fix the dose of stillness.

progression.rule: In-range progression; stretches by comfort range.
progression.deload: Not needed at this volume.

programs.scienceRationale: "Posture correction" is less about stretching into a shape and more about building capacity in the neglected pulling and hip-extension patterns plus breaking up sedentary time — prolonged uninterrupted sitting shows dose-response links with musculoskeletal complaints, and regular activity breaks plus strengthening reduce neck/shoulder pain in office workers in controlled trials. The 2:1 pull bias rebalances the pressing-and-hunching default.
evidence: Strength training reduces neck and shoulder pain in desk workers
Exercise is the most reliable treatment for persistent neck pain
Breaking up long stretches of sitting matters independently of the workout itself
programs.expectedResults: Less end-of-day stiffness within 2-3 weeks; visibly better standing posture by week 8 — because the muscles that hold it finally can.
programs.cautions: The hourly movement snack outperforms any 40-minute session you follow with 9 frozen hours.

programs.name: First Reps: Teen Training Foundations
programs.whoIsItFor: Teenagers starting structured training — technique-first, bodyweight-forward, building the habit and the movement library before chasing load.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody in the age band — resistance training is safe and beneficial for adolescents under sensible supervision; growth-plate fear is a myth under proper technique and progression.

slots.variant: jump/hop variety: lateral, single-leg low hops

programs.schedule: Around school sport — this plan yields to practices and matches, never stacks on them.

progression.rule: Load enters only after 15 flawless bodyweight/light reps; every progression is earned by form, never by ego. A rep-in-reserve buffer is permanent at this age.
progression.deload: Exam weeks: one session is a win.

programs.scienceRationale: Position statements from pediatric sports-medicine bodies endorse supervised resistance training for adolescents as safe and beneficial — injury rates are low and lower than most field sports — with technique competence gating load. Adolescence is also a high-payoff window for motor-skill breadth and jumping/landing mechanics, which is why variety and landing quality get dedicated slots.
evidence: The international consensus is that supervised youth resistance training is safe and valuable
Supervised resistance training is safe and beneficial for young athletes
Coaching landing mechanics early prevents knee injuries later
programs.expectedResults: A teenager who moves well, has baseline strength, and — the real outcome — likes training enough to keep going.
programs.cautions: The one hard rule: no maxing out. Rep buffers stay, full stop.

programs.name: Carry-On: Hotel Room Maintenance
programs.whoIsItFor: Frequent travelers who want to hold their gains from a hotel room in 20 minutes — zero equipment, optional light band that fits any bag.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody — this is a maintenance bridge, not a destination.

days.name: The circuit (all days — 3-4 rounds, minimal rest, ~20 min)

slots.variant: pushup — hardest variant available (feet on bed = decline)
band row (door anchor) or towel-doorframe row

programs.schedule: Every other morning of the trip, before the day eats you. Walk everywhere the trip allows.

progression.rule: Same circuit, one more round or less rest — this plan maintains, it doesn't need to build.
progression.deload: It is one.

programs.scienceRationale: Muscle and strength are far cheaper to keep than to build — maintenance requires roughly a third (or less) of building volume, and short-term detraining losses in 1-2 weeks are minimal and mostly fluid. Three brief near-failure full-body exposures a week comfortably clear the retention threshold, so the trip costs nothing.
evidence: Keeping muscle takes roughly a third of the volume it took to build it
Strength holds for weeks without training; conditioning fades sooner
programs.expectedResults: Come home at the strength you left with, minus the usual travel guilt.
programs.cautions: Doorframe rows: test the door's swing direction before trusting it with your bodyweight.

programs.name: Band Together: Resistance-Band Full Program
programs.whoIsItFor: Home trainees whose entire gym is a set of loop/tube bands — a real program, not a compromise, up to the point band tension runs out.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Intermediate+ lower-body strength (leg tension ceilings arrive fast — see the dumbbell or gym plans).

slots.variant: band chest press (anchor) or banded pushup

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive days; anchor-point setup notes live with the plan, not in your memory.

progression.rule: Reps to the range top -> next band up or double bands or widen stance/shorten band; last-3-reps-hard is the calibration test each set.
progression.deload: Week 5: 2 sets per slot.

programs.scienceRationale: Elastic-resistance training produces strength and hypertrophy gains comparable to conventional resistance in beginners and intermediates when effort is matched — the muscle registers tension near failure, not the tool providing it. Bands' ascending resistance even biases the easier joint angles harder, and high-rep near-failure sets sit squarely in the load-independent hypertrophy evidence.
evidence: Bands build strength comparably to free weights when the effort matches
Light and heavy loads build similar muscle when sets are taken close to failure
programs.expectedResults: Beginner/novice gains fully comparable to dumbbells for the first months; lower body outgrows bands first.
programs.cautions: Inspect bands for nicks — a snapped band at face height is the sport's only real injury.
