programs.name: Any-Hour: Shift Worker's Flexible Plan
programs.whoIsItFor: Nurses, drivers, hospitality, security — anyone whose week has no fixed shape. Three interchangeable sessions, no fixed days, with a readiness rule replacing a schedule.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody; the design is the accommodation.

days.name: Session 1 (do these in rotation, whenever you can)

programs.schedule: No days — a rotation counter (1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1). Rules: never two sessions within 24h; a session straight off a night shift runs at RPE 7 cap; 4+ days without training -> just do the next session, no makeups.

progression.rule: In-range progression on good days; post-night-shift sessions hold weight and bank reps. Progress happens on the rested days.
progression.deload: A brutal rota IS a deload — the plan absorbs it by design.

programs.scienceRationale: Shift work degrades recovery via circadian disruption and sleep debt, which argues for autoregulation over fixed loading — RPE-capped sessions after night shifts respect measurably reduced neuromuscular readiness while keeping the training frequency that protects fitness. Rotation-based structure removes the adherence-killing mismatch between a Monday/Wednesday/Friday plan and a life without Mondays.
evidence: Shift work disrupts sleep, and training has to be planned around it rather than through it
Loading by felt effort fits the session to the day you actually turned up with
Short sleep blunts recovery and the adaptation training has earned
programs.expectedResults: Consistent progress despite an inconsistent life — slower on paper than a fixed plan, infinitely faster than the fixed plan you kept abandoning.
programs.cautions: The RPE 7 post-nights cap is load management, not weakness — fatigue misjudges weights.

programs.name: Down Week: Active Recovery Template
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone due a deload: post-program, post-race, run-down, or just flat for two weeks straight. One week that lets adaptation catch up without going still.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody — but if every week feels like it needs to be this week, the problem is the program (or the sleep), not the deload.

slots.variant: anything enjoyable and easy: swim, bike, hike, kickabout

programs.schedule: One week, then back to programming. Sleep is the main event; this is its supporting act.

progression.rule: Nothing progresses this week on purpose — that's the entire mechanism.
progression.deload: This is one.

programs.scienceRationale: Planned volume reductions dissipate accumulated neuromuscular and perceptual fatigue while fitness barely moves — the taper literature shows performance typically rises after 40-60% volume cuts — and light activity beats full rest for soreness and mood. A deload spends one week to buy the next block's quality.
evidence: A planned taper before a test raises performance on the day
Light movement clears fatigue better than complete rest
Performance is fitness minus fatigue, so fatigue is managed rather than merely accumulated
programs.expectedResults: Week after: weights feel lighter, motivation returns, small PRs are common.
programs.cautions: The urge to sneak in one hard set on Thursday is the test. Pass it.

programs.name: Center of Mass: 6-Week Core Project
programs.whoIsItFor: Anyone who wants a genuinely strong trunk — bracing, anti-rotation, carrying, and yes, visible abs if the diet cooperates. Runs standalone (3x/week) or bolted onto any strength plan (the day-3 add-on).
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Acute low-back flare-ups start with a clinician, not a core program.

slots.variant: plank ladder: standard -> long-lever -> body saw
pallof press ladder: kneeling -> standing -> split stance
side plank ladder: knees -> full -> leg lifted

programs.schedule: Standalone: 3 non-consecutive days. Add-on mode: appended to existing sessions, one day each.

progression.rule: Each drill has a listed ladder — advance a rung when the current one hits target time/reps with quality; loaded moves by load.
progression.deload: Not needed at 25 min.

programs.scienceRationale: Trunk function is mostly anti-motion — resisting extension, rotation, and lateral flexion under load — so the program is organized around those categories rather than crunch volume, per the spine-stability research tradition. Loaded carries and integration lifts convert isolated capacity into usable stiffness, and the rectus still gets direct flexion work because it's a muscle like any other and responds to progressive overload.
evidence: The trunk's real job is resisting motion, not creating it
Trained directly and progressively, the core responds like any other muscle group
The abs grow from progressive overload like any other muscle
programs.expectedResults: Noticeably stronger bracing under squats/deadlifts, sturdier single-leg balance, and a trunk that looks like it trains.
programs.cautions: Visible abs are made in the kitchen; this builds what the deficit reveals.

programs.name: 13.1: Half Marathon Builder
programs.whoIsItFor: Runners stepping up from 10K to a strong first (or faster next) half marathon in 12 weeks.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Anyone straight off the couch — the 5K and 10K plans are the on-ramp; skipping them is how tibias file complaints.

slots.variant: alternates weekly: tempo (25-35 min comfortably hard) / cruise intervals (4-5 x 8 min at threshold, 2 min jog)

slots.reps: wk1: 80 min -> peak wk10: 110-120 min (last 15 min at goal pace from wk6) -> wk12 taper: 60 min

programs.schedule: Long run + next day easy or rest; down-weeks (-25% volume) at weeks 4 and 8; 10-day taper into race day.

progression.rule: Weekly volume +8-10% between down-weeks; goal-pace segments grow inside the long run from week 6 — race rehearsal, fueling included.
progression.deload: Weeks 4, 8, and the taper.

programs.scienceRationale: Half-marathon performance rides on lactate threshold and fatigue-resistant aerobic volume: cruise intervals and tempos push the threshold ceiling while the progressively longer long run — with goal-pace finishing segments — builds the specific endurance and fueling practice the distance demands. The 80%-easy distribution and scheduled down-weeks manage the injury risk that rises with half-marathon mileage.
evidence: Roughly 80% easy and 20% hard beats training everything in the middle
Threshold work is the highest-value running intensity per hour spent
Running injuries track sudden jumps in weekly volume more than volume itself
programs.expectedResults: A completed half at even pace — or for repeat racers, typically minutes off the previous time.
programs.cautions: Nothing new on race day: shoes, breakfast, and gels all get rehearsed on long-run Sundays first.

programs.name: Selection Ready: Tactical Fitness Test Prep
programs.whoIsItFor: Candidates prepping for military, police, or fire-service fitness tests — the classic battery: push-ups, sit-ups/plank, pull-ups, a 2-3K run, sometimes a loaded march.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Under 8 weeks from a base of zero running — extend the timeline rather than compress the ramp.

slots.variant: test-spec: sit-ups or plank per your battery

slots.reps: 2 min at target test pace, 90s jog

slots.variant: easy run, or loaded march if your test has one (10-15kg)

days.name: Full mock test (every 2nd week) / hinge strength (alternate)

slots.variant: MOCK: full test battery under test conditions and rest periods

programs.schedule: Mock test every second week calibrates everything; final mock no closer than 10 days out, then taper.

progression.rule: Calisthenics progress by density (more sub-failure volume), never by testing daily; run by holding target pace for longer reps. The mock is the only max-out.
progression.deload: Final 10 days: -50% volume, keep pace touches.

programs.scienceRationale: Test performance is a skill of specific repeatability: high-frequency sub-failure calisthenics volume (grease-the-groove) reliably outgrows test-to-failure training for push-up and pull-up scores, interval work at exactly test pace develops the specific speed-endurance the run scores demand, and biweekly mocks give pacing calibration plus objective progression data.
evidence: Frequent, sub-maximal practice builds skill faster than occasional all-out efforts
You get good at what you practise — training has to resemble the goal
Stopping a rep or two short preserves the quality of every set that follows
programs.expectedResults: Typical 8-week outcomes: +20-40% push-up/pull-up scores and a materially faster test run versus baseline mock.
programs.cautions: Rucking progresses load OR distance, never both in the same week — hips and feet keep the receipts.

programs.name: First Chair: Ski & Snowboard Prep
programs.whoIsItFor: Skiers and snowboarders who want legs that last past lunch on day one and knees that survive the season — run it the 8 weeks before the first trip.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Existing ACL rehab belongs with a physio; this is prevention and prep, not rehab.

slots.intensity: RPE 8 — slow descents are the ski-specific part

slots.variant: lateral bounds, stick each landing (skater jumps)

slots.intensity: silent landings, knees track over toes
the exact quad burn of a long run

programs.schedule: Non-consecutive; the plyometric day is the priority if a week collapses to two sessions.

progression.rule: Weeks 1-4 build eccentric strength and landing quality; weeks 5-8 add reactive elements (jump variations, longer wall sits). Peak week is the week before the trip, not during it.
progression.deload: Travel week: mobility only.

programs.scienceRationale: Skiing is quasi-isometric and eccentric quad work in fatigue — hence tempo eccentrics and wall-sit ladders — and its signature injury is the ACL, whose prevention evidence centers on landing mechanics, lateral control, and hamstring strength, all given dedicated slots. Interval conditioning buys altitude and full-day tolerance.
evidence: Structured neuromuscular warm-ups measurably cut ACL injuries
Skiing is mostly eccentric and isometric leg work, so the training should be too
The first hard session is the sorest — one exposure protects against the next
programs.expectedResults: Day-one legs that last to last lift, faster recovery between ski days, meaningfully lowered knee-injury risk profile.
programs.cautions: The plan ends before the trip on purpose — arriving fresh beats arriving trained-and-trashed.

programs.name: Send Support: Climber's Antagonist & Base
programs.whoIsItFor: Boulderers and route climbers who climb 2-4x weekly and need the complement: pushing strength, shoulder balance, legs, and elbow care. Deliberately NOT more pulling — the wall provides that.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody climbing regularly; finger-injury rehab specifics belong with a climbing physio.

slots.intensity: RPE 8 — high-step strength is free grade

slots.variant: hip mobility: deep goblet hold + frog

programs.schedule: On non-climbing days or after easy sessions — never before a hard session (fresh fingers outrank everything).

progression.rule: In-range progression; antagonist work stays 2+ reps from failure permanently — it supports climbing, it doesn't compete with it.
progression.deload: Trip weeks and peak projects: day 1 only, half sets.

programs.scienceRationale: Climbing overdevelops pulling and finger flexion, and the sport's chronic elbow and shoulder complaints track that imbalance — antagonist strengthening (pushing, wrist extension, external rotation) is the standard evidence-informed countermeasure. Leg and hip work is climbing's cheapest performance upgrade: strong high-steps and hip mobility unload the fingers directly.
evidence: Climbing injuries concentrate in the finger pulleys and shoulders
Climbers need pushing work to balance a sport made entirely of pulling
Climbing injuries are prevented by training the antagonists the wall never works
programs.expectedResults: Quieter elbows and shoulders, sturdier shoulders on gastons and mantles, and better footwork strength inside 10 weeks.
programs.cautions: This program never touches a hangboard — finger loading belongs in your climbing plan, not stacked here.

programs.name: Tri Curious: Sprint Triathlon Finisher

audience.prerequisite: Can swim 200m (any pace, breaks OK), ride 30 min, run/walk 20 min

programs.whoIsItFor: First-timers targeting a sprint triathlon (~750m swim / 20K bike / 5K run) in 8 weeks — finishing strong, not podium chasing.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Non-swimmers: get lessons first — open-water readiness is a safety line, not a fitness line.

slots.reps: wk1: 8x50m easy w/ rest -> wk7: 3x300m steady
wk1: 40 min -> wk7: 70 min with 3x8 min race-effort surges from wk4

days.name: Swim 2 (open-water skills from wk5 where possible)

slots.variant: sighting practice, continuous swimming, wetsuit if race uses one

slots.intensity: RPE 6 — jelly legs are the point; they improve

programs.schedule: Brick weekly (it's the sport's signature adaptation); week 8 halves everything, race weekend caps it. Practice transitions at home: it's free minutes.

progression.rule: One discipline progresses volume per week in rotation; the brick's run segment grows steadily. Down-week at week 4.
progression.deload: Week 4 and race-week taper.

programs.scienceRationale: Sprint-distance success for novices is about frequency across three disciplines at mostly easy intensity plus the bike-to-run transition adaptation — the brick — which trains the well-documented neuromuscular and perceptual awkwardness of running off the bike. Open-water skills (sighting, contact, wetsuit swimming) are practiced because race-day swim anxiety, not fitness, is the novice's biggest documented stressor.
evidence: Multisport hours are distributed by the demands of each discipline, not split evenly
The bike-to-run transition is a trainable skill in its own right
Open water demands its own safety skills before any distance is added
programs.expectedResults: Cross the line running, not surviving — and probably hooked.
programs.cautions: Never swim open water alone in training. No exceptions.

programs.name: Daily Fifteen: Morning Movement Habit
programs.whoIsItFor: People who want a daily, sustainable, no-decisions morning routine — the anchor habit that makes everything else easier. Runs alongside any other plan or alone.
programs.whoShouldAvoid: Nobody — it's scaled by effort, not by fitness.

days.name: The routine (same every day — that's the design)

slots.variant: optional finisher: 2 min brisk march or step outside for light

programs.schedule: Every morning, same order, before the phone. Weekend version identical — that's what makes it a habit, not a program.

progression.rule: For 4 weeks the only metric is days completed. After the streak holds, nudge reps or add a harder variant — but never at the cost of the streak.
progression.deload: Sick days: do the first two drills in pajamas and count it. Chain preserved.

programs.scienceRationale: Habit formation research favors identical cues, identical routines, and low activation cost — a same-time same-sequence morning routine exploits exactly that, and consistency beats intensity for the health returns of daily movement. Morning light and brief activity also support circadian phase and mood, and 15 daily minutes clears meaningful minimum-activity thresholds on its own.
evidence: A new habit takes roughly two months of repetition before it runs itself
Habit-based routines outlast motivation-based ones
Morning light and movement anchor the body clock and lift mood
programs.expectedResults: A 28-day chain, better mornings, and the platform habit other training gets built on.
programs.cautions: The rule that saves it: a bad version of the routine always beats a skipped one.
